subject: ss-infectious-diseases
title: Adult immunization: pneumococcal, zoster, influenza and live vaccine safety

steps.tx: **Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV)** is non-live and contains an adjuvanted glycoprotein E antigen. It is given as two doses, usually two to six months apart, to adults aged 50 and older, including those with prior herpes zoster. Immunocompromised adults may receive the second dose sooner, after one to two months. Because it is non-live, it is safe in immunosuppressed patients, unlike live zoster vaccine. Vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster remains high across age groups.

steps.tx: The photo shows clustered clear **blisters on red skin** confined to one band across the back, the classic **dermatomal rash** of shingles after varicella reactivation. This painful eruption is what **recombinant zoster vaccine** prevents in adults from age fifty onward, given as two doses months apart, and it remains suitable when immunity is weak because it contains no live virus.
steps.say: This back shows grouped blisters on reddened skin in a single stripe on one side, the textbook look of shingles. Shingles follows reactivation of the chickenpox virus along one nerve territory. The lesson pairs this picture with recombinant zoster vaccine, a non live option for adults from age fifty, given in two doses, which stays safe when immunity is suppressed.

steps.tx: **Influenza vaccine** is given every year to all adults, with the strain matched to circulating viruses. Inactivated vaccine is safe in pregnancy, chronic illness and immunosuppression. **Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV)** is avoided in pregnancy, immunocompromised patients and those in close contact with severely immunosuppressed people. Guillain-Barre syndrome has been reported after influenza vaccination, but the absolute risk is very small compared with influenza illness itself.

steps.tx: **Live vaccines** contain replicating organisms and are contraindicated in **severe immunosuppression**, pregnancy and within a short window after high-dose corticosteroids or blood products. Examples include MMR, varicella, yellow fever, oral Ty21a typhoid and LAIV. Inactivated, recombinant and toxoid vaccines are generally safe for immunocompromised patients, though responses may be weaker. Immunocompromised patients should be vaccinated before immunosuppression where possible.
steps.say: Live vaccines contain replicating organisms and are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression, in pregnancy, and within a short window after high-dose corticosteroids or blood products. Examples include MMR, varicella, yellow fever, oral Ty21a typhoid and live attenuated influenza vaccine. Inactivated, recombinant and toxoid vaccines are generally safe for immunocompromised patients, though responses may be weaker. Where possible, vaccinate before immunosuppression starts.

steps.tx: Hepatitis B **non-responders** are adults who do not reach protective **anti-HBs** levels after a full three-dose series. Check anti-HBs one to two months after the final dose. If the level is low, a repeat **three-dose series** is given, with antibodies checked again. Persistent non-response suggests testing for **HBsAg** and anti-HBc, and considering a booster or referral. Separately, Tdap is given in every pregnancy, timed for the later part of gestation, to protect the newborn against **pertussis**.
